newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Italy's EMU drive alarms some of its partners.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy's EMU drive alarms some of its partners.

text.p: For all the talk of who will qualify for monetary union and whether it will happen on time, the big question has more to do with emotion than economics -- are people prepared to trust the Italians in a shared currency?

Economists say that despite its latest political crisis, Italy is beginning to show every sign it can squeeze into the euro when it is launched in 1999, alarming some central bankers and leaving politicians floundering for a response.
"The question of Italian membership will be the key question for 1997," said a recent study by a think-tank set up by former European Commission president Jacques Delors.
The German Bundesbank, fearing early Italian membership would weaken the single currency, is seen as the staunchest opponent, supported by some other hardline central bankers.
"The Germans, who want a strong euro, in my opinion too strong a euro, tend to reject the southern countries," Bank of France council member Paul Marchelli told Reuters on Friday.
"They fear the euro will not be strong enough. It is the only real problem for the Italians."
Marchelli, known for views that are often at odds with the government or Bank of France, said founding EU member Italy, along with Spain and Portugal must be in from the start.
"I cannot imagine the euro without Italy. It is impossible. It is like having Paris without the Eiffel Tower," he said.

Opponents of Italian membership have hoped that Italy would disqualify itself by failing to meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria for membership of economic and monetary union (EMU), economists say they are showing signs that this game plan might not work.

"I get the feeling that a number of central bankers are becoming quite hysterical because they never expected Italy to get in," Bernard Godement, senior economist at Daiwa Institute of Research Europe, said.

Some economists say they sense the stepping up of a "dirty campaign" to keep Italy out, which started with the labelling of Italy, Spain and Portugal as "Club Med" countries -- more suitable as holiday destinations than shared currency partners.

Now, by dropping heavy hints that Rome is unwelcome, opponents of Italian membership are seen as keeping up pressure on the lira and Italian interest rates, making it harder for Italy to meet Maastricht criteria.
Italy's budget would be in surplus without its big debt service charges and rate cuts would allow it to cut its deficit.
"The key for the budget deficit problem is interest rates," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.

But even if Italy meets the Maastricht criteria, it must still overcome fears its membership of EMU would make the euro less credible in the eyes of investors who would then demand a higher risk premium in the form of higher interest rates.
This week's political crisis, during which Prime Minister Romano Prodi threatened to resign in a row over the deployment of Italian forces to Albania, was only a small addition to that mistrust.
More important are fears that having gone on a crash diet to meet the Maastricht targets it will regain weight later.
And that has led to an insistence that sustainability of deficit reduction must be taken into account when the EU leaders decide, probably in May 1998, who can join the single currency.
"The fact that Italy has a huge debt ratio is a consequence of many years of bad management," Darren Williams, economist at UBS in London, said. "It's a question of trust," he said.
That view has to be squared with an argument by Italy, Spain and Portugal that they signed Maastricht in good faith and that what counts is not trust but meeting the criteria.

France, meanwhile, is keeping a very low profile, avoiding for the most part the kind of public comments it made last year when it warned against an overly strong euro, and said the currency should not become "the plaything" of central banks.
But many see President Jacques Chirac caught between a French cultural affinity with Italy and the need to stay on good terms with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
The Socialist party, making the question an issue for the March 1998 parliamentary elections, has already said it wants Italy, Spain and Portugal in EMU from the start.
"It seems to me that the French do not have any fundamental position. Chirac is not really going to struggle hard with Germany to get the Italians in but the game is not over yet," Brossard said.
"For most French people, Italy is one of the first European countries, much more than Germany," he added.
